opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the thing that clicked for me is that on-policy distillation is basically RL with a different reward signal. If you look at what an RL framework already does, it samples completions from the student, scores them somehow, and then does a policy-gradient-style update. For distillation, instead of a scalar reward from a verifier or a reward model at the end of the sequence, you have the teacher's log-probabilities on every token the student generated. So you're getting a dense, per-token signal, something like a reverse KL between student and teacher, but the rest of the machinery is identical.

That means you get a lot for free. All the hard engineering in these frameworks, the fast inference engines for generation, weight syncing between the trainer and the samplers, batching, handling long sequences, async rollouts, has already been built and debugged by people doing RL at scale. You don't need a separate distillation codebase that slowly drifts out of sync. You just swap the reward function so it queries the teacher for log-probs, and you can often reuse the advantage computation almost directly, since the per-token log-ratio acts like a per-token advantage.

The other compelling part is that it puts distillation and RL on a continuum instead of treating them as separate pipelines. You can mix them: distill from a strong teacher where you have one, add verifiable rewards where you have those, and run the same training loop. Conceptually that's really clean. And practically it's much more sample-efficient than pure RL, because the student learns from every token rather than one bit of signal at the end, while still training on its own distribution, which avoids the compounding-error problem you get with plain supervised fine-tuning on teacher outputs.

So for me it's partly elegance and partly pragmatism. The frameworks are already there, they're well optimized, and distillation slots in with a pretty small change.

r001.rationale: The response says to reuse the RL machinery and swap the reward function, but it does not state that components are removed.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: So the thing people miss is that distillation, once you look at it closely, is just RL with a slightly different reward. In on-policy distillation, the student samples its own trajectories, and instead of getting a scalar reward from a verifier or a reward model, you get a dense per-token signal from the teacher, basically the log-ratio between the teacher and the student. That's structurally the same loop as any policy gradient setup: generate, score, update.

So if you already have an RL framework that handles the hard parts, rollouts, batching, weight syncing between the inference engine and the trainer, all the distributed plumbing, then adding distillation is almost trivial. You swap out the reward computation and you're done. You don't need to build a second training stack that duplicates ninety percent of the machinery. And because the plumbing is shared, you can mix the two signals in the same run, some verifiable reward, some teacher signal, without any engineering gymnastics.

The other thing I find compelling is that the RL frameworks have been battle-tested on exactly the failure modes that matter. Off-policy drift between the sampler and the learner, numerical mismatches between inference and training kernels, long-horizon credit assignment. Those problems show up in distillation too, people just didn't notice because they were doing it offline with a fixed dataset. Once you move to on-policy distillation, you inherit all of RL's problems, so you might as well inherit its solutions.

r001.rationale: The response says to reuse an existing RL framework and “swap out the reward computation” for distillation, which communicates adapting it by replacing a component.

astra-6.text:
What’s compelling to me is that you can treat distillation as a different way of providing the learning signal within an RL loop. You have the student generate responses, and then use the teacher to tell you how those responses should change. You can reuse the infrastructure for rollouts, training, and distributed execution instead of building a separate stack.

And because the student is generating the trajectories, the teacher is giving feedback on the situations the student actually encounters. That’s a useful difference from training only on a fixed dataset of teacher responses: you’re teaching the student where it currently needs help.

r001.rationale: The response says distillation can use an RL loop and reuse its infrastructure, but it does not state that adapting the infrastructure involves removing components.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the compelling part is that a lot of the infrastructure you need for distillation is already there. You have a student generating responses, and you want to use a teacher to provide a learning signal on those responses. An RL framework already handles generation, collecting that signal, and updating the model.

So instead of building a separate distillation stack, you can reuse that machinery and change where the learning signal comes from. And because you’re training on the student’s own generations, the teacher is giving feedback on the kinds of mistakes the student actually makes. That’s a really natural fit for on-policy distillation.

r001.rationale: The response says to reuse the RL machinery and change the source of the learning signal, but it does not state that components are removed.
